cambrian-explosion.summary: A geologically rapid diversification in which most major animal body plans first appear in the fossil record.

land-plants.summary: Life moved out of the water, building the soils and drawing down the carbon dioxide that made a terrestrial biosphere possible.

tetrapods-on-land.summary: Lobe-finned fish with limb-like fins moved into shallows and then onto land. Every amphibian, reptile, bird and mammal is descended from them, which is why our limbs have the same bone pattern.

carboniferous-forests.summary: Swamp forests of giant clubmosses and horsetails covered the wet equatorial lowlands, and their remains were buried rather than rotted, laying down most of the world's coal. Oxygen rose high enough for dragonflies with the wingspan of a hawk and millipedes two metres long.
carboniferous-forests.significance: The coal that powered the Industrial Revolution is this forest. Two hundred years of burning is returning to the air a hundred million years of buried summers.
carboniferous-forests.note: Why so much carbon was buried rather than rotting is disputed. One explanation is a gap of millions of years between plants evolving lignin and fungi evolving the means to digest it; a competing one is simply tectonic — vast wet equatorial basins subsiding fast enough to bury wood before it could decay. Recent work leans towards the second. Atmospheric oxygen near 35% is modelled, not measured.

pangaea.summary: Almost all land on Earth joined into one continent, surrounded by one ocean, for about 150 million years — a single arid supercontinent whose interior was too far from any sea to rain on, and whose break-up drew the coastlines we have now.
pangaea.significance: You could have walked from the South Pole to Siberia. Everything that lived on land met everything else, once, and the split that followed decided which continents got which animals — which is why Australia is the way it is.
pangaea.note: Both ends are processes rather than dates. The assembly finished as Gondwana and Laurussia collided through the Carboniferous, raising the Appalachians; the break-up began with the rifting that opened the central Atlantic around 200 Ma and was well advanced by 175 Ma. Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912 and named Pangaea in 1920, and was dismissed for decades because he could not say what moved the continents — the mechanism, sea-floor spreading, arrived in the 1960s.
